title: The Mongols
hook: armies from the steppe sweep through Central Asia and Persia

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jerusalem, a ransom at the gate, and some who couldn't pay set free. Your line was mercy in victory.

A caravan of merchants rides into a border town called Otrar, on the eastern edge of the lands of the Khwarazm-shah. They've come from the ruler of the steppe peoples, to trade. As the chroniclers tell it, the town's governor accuses them of being spies and has them killed. An envoy comes to complain, and he is killed too. A quarrel over goods and pride on a frontier, the kind of thing a governor might expect to forget. It was not forgotten. Today: the Mongols.
screen: `MERCHANTS RIDE INTO OTRAR.` → `KILLED AS SPIES.` → `IT WAS NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: The Mongols were peoples of the steppe, the wide grasslands north of China, horsemen brought under one ruler, Chinggis Khan. After Otrar, their armies came west, through Bukhara and Samarkand, cities of mosques, markets and scholars, and on into Persia. The chronicles describe cities that resisted and were emptied, and cities that opened their gates and were spared. They are hard reading. The historian Ibn al-Athir was writing a great history of the world in Mosul when the news arrived. He writes that he held back from writing this part for a long while, because he could not bear to. When he did, he said he wished he had died before it happened and been forgotten, words that echo Mary's cry in surah Maryam. A historian whose job was to write everything down, wishing he hadn't lived to write this. That's today's line: the storm from the east. It's a picture, not a weather report: how it felt to people who had no way to stop it. So what does a believer say when the news is that bad? You met the words at Jerusalem's fall; here is where they come from. Surah al-Baqarah describes those who, when misfortune strikes, say, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." In Arabic: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Muslims say it at a death, and at any loss or bad news, large or small. It doesn't explain the storm, or pretend it isn't happening. It simply says who the grieving belong to while it passes over.
screen: `RIDERS FROM THE STEPPE.` · `BUKHARA, SAMARKAND, PERSIA.` · `A HISTORIAN WHO COULDN'T WRITE IT.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND TO HIM WE RETURN.` · then, large: `THE STORM FROM THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place where people are living through war right now, and let one person there become clear: a grandmother who can't leave, a child who knows the sound of planes, a doctor who hasn't slept. If you pray, ask Allah for their safety and for help to reach them; if you don't, simply keep them in mind, and don't look away early.
The Mongols. Horsemen of the steppe, united under Chinggis Khan, whose armies swept through Central Asia and Persia. Today's word.
Your line: the storm from the east. Next, the storm reaches Baghdad. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, from surah al-Baqarah, when they hear of a death or any loss, and Friday sermons sometimes close with supplications for people suffering war.

options: Inna lillahi: we are Allah's and to Him we are returning.
Nothing; grief over loss is seen as a lack of faith.
A prayer explaining exactly why the disaster happened.
chat.meaning: Al-Baqarah describes those who, when misfortune strikes, say: we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning. It doesn't explain the storm.
